Structures and Function

Where we are going

Learning Outcomes

Roadmap

By the end you can

  • Locate the heart chambers, valves, and great vessels relevant to electrophysiology
  • Describe the conduction components (SA node, AV node, His bundle, Purkinje fibers) and their roles
  • Explain, in concept, how the electrical impulse spreads through the heart and triggers contraction
  • Identify the cardiac cell types and what each does
  • Relate the electrical activity to the mechanical cardiac cycle
  • Read basic ECG components (P, QRS, T) and what they represent
  • Explain the fibrous skeleton as structural support and electrical insulation
  • Apply the anatomy to common arrhythmias and their treatment

04

Bridge

First, Review Normal Conduction

Set the stage

To understand Jack and test your prediction, we first need to review how the heart normally conducts an impulse.

  • Build the normal system, structure by structure, top to apex
  • See what each part does and how fast it can fire
  • Then return to Jack and find exactly where his signal breaks
05

Why it exists

Purpose of the Conduction System

Big picture

The job, top to bottom

Ultimate goal: generate the blood pressure and cardiac output that deliver oxygen-rich blood to the organs.

  • The chambers of the heart are pumps
  • The conduction system generates the electrical impulses that make myocardial cells contract, and so the chambers pump
  • Right timing matters: the atria must finish filling the ventricles before the ventricles fire
04

Physiology

Two Types of Cardiac Cells

Cells

Contractile cells (cardiac muscle)

  • Do the pumping when the conduction system stimulates them
  • Propagate the action potential along the sarcolemma
  • Each heartbeat, muscle contracts twice: once in the atria, once in the ventricles

Non-contractile cells (nodal)

  • Specialized cells that fire an action potential on their own: automaticity
  • They do not contract
Key idea: nodal cells set the rhythm, contractile cells do the work. Every nodal level can fire on its own, which is what saves Jack later.
05

Anatomy

The Pathway and the Pacemakers

Trace it

One signal, top to apex

  • SA node fires, sweeps the atria (the P wave)
  • Signal reaches the AV node, the only electrical door, which adds a delay
  • Down the bundle of His, into the right and left bundle branches along the septum
  • Out the Purkinje fibers at the apex, up the ventricular walls (the QRS)
  • The fibrous skeleton blocks every other route between atria and ventricles
StructureIntrinsic rate
SA node60 to 100
AV node / His40 to 55
Purkinje / ventricle25 to 40
The fastest pacemaker wins. The SA node fires quickest, so it keeps resetting the slower pacemakers before they can fire, and normally we feel only the SA node (overdrive suppression). A slower pacemaker takes over, an escape rhythm, only if the faster signal fails or cannot reach it, which is exactly what rescues Jack's ventricles.
06

Pacemaker 1

Sinoatrial (SA) Node

Primary

The natural pacemaker of the heart

  • Function: initiates and coordinates the timing of contraction. These cells do not contract; they give the contracting cells the signal
  • Automaticity: fires without external input
  • Intrinsic rate: 60 to 100 bpm. Transmits to both atria and the AV node
  • Location: junction of the right atrium and the superior vena cava
  • Blood supply: SA nodal artery, a branch of the right coronary artery (about 68 percent); left circumflex in about 24 percent
Clinical relevance: because the SA node is usually fed by the right coronary artery, an inferior (right coronary) heart attack can disturb the pacemaker and the rhythm.
07

Pacemaker 2

Atrioventricular (AV) Node

The gate

The secondary pacemaker and the delay

  • Function: stimulated by the SA node, then transmits to the bundle of His
  • Creates a deliberate delay so the atria finish filling the ventricles before they fire
  • Intrinsic rate: 40 to 55 bpm
  • Location: base of the interatrial septum, just above the tricuspid valve, near the opening of the coronary sinus
  • Blood supply: AV nodal artery, most commonly a branch of the right coronary artery
08

The wiring

Bundle of His and Bundle Branches

Staircase

From the gate down the septum

  • Bundle of His arises from the AV node and runs along the interventricular septum; it helps prevent backward conduction
  • It divides into the right and left bundle branches, which run down the septum toward the apex
  • They transmit the impulse to the walls of the ventricles
  • Intrinsic rate: 40 to 55 bpm
09

The wiring

Purkinje Fibers

Last mile

Subendocardial fibers

  • Function: arise from the bundle branches and spread the impulse rapidly through the ventricular muscle
  • Location: begin at the apex, then continue up the walls of the ventricles
  • Intrinsic rate: 25 to 40 bpm, the slowest backup in the system
  • This bottom-up spread wrings the ventricles out toward the great vessels
10

The insulation

Fibrous Skeleton of the Heart

Structure

Dense irregular connective tissue

  • Mechanical support at the boundary between atria and ventricles
  • Forms fibrous rings that anchor the valves
  • Framework for cardiac muscle attachment, like wringing out a mop
  • Electrical insulation: a shield that prevents action potentials from passing directly from atria to ventricles, so they do not contract at the same time
Discuss in your teams: why might the fibrous skeleton matter for Jack?

P and QRS never line up

Normal: every P drags a QRS with it. Jack: the P waves (about 80) and QRS complexes (about 38) run on separate clocks. That dissociation is the diagnosis.

12

Apply it

Your Call

Application

Question 1

The backup rate tells you where the break is. Jack escapes at 38. Is his block more likely high or low?

The answer

Low. A high block (at the AV node) leaves a junctional backup of 40 to 55. A low block (His-Purkinje) leaves only the ventricular backup of 25 to 40. Jack's 38 is low, so his rate points to where the failure lives.

Question 2

You can place one pacing wire. Where does it belong?

The answer

The ventricle, at the right ventricular apex. The break is below the AV node, so pacing above it changes nothing. You drive the ventricles directly, which is what a pacemaker does: an artificial route past the broken door.

13

Resolution

Back to Jack

Tie it together

Third degree (complete) heart block

  • The AV door is shut. Atrial signals reach it and stop, so the atria keep firing near 80 (the marching P waves)
  • Cut off, the ventricles fall back on their own escape rhythm, 25 to 40. Jack lands at 38
  • Most likely cause here: not an acute heart attack but age-related degenerative scarring of the His-Purkinje system, an infranodal block. The slow escape of 38 and the need to pace the ventricle both place the lesion below the AV node
  • Only ventricular beats eject blood, so his output drops, his brain comes up short, and he faints in the garden
  • The fix drives the ventricles directly with a pacemaker, a new route past the broken door
The whole goal: trace any beat from the SA node, through the atria, down the AV node and His-Purkinje system to the apex, and when something breaks, predict both the rhythm and where the problem sits.
